The category printed on the cable describes tested cabling performance. The slowest port, cable path, or device sets the link speed.

:::: {.tej-visual-grid}
::: {.tej-visual-card}
![Numbered contacts on an 8P8C modular plug.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/file/Rj45plug-8p8c.png)

### 8P8C, often called RJ45

Eight positions and eight contacts. Keep the pairs twisted close to the plug. Do not judge cable category by colour.

*Figure 1. [Open source and licence.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rj45plug-8p8c.png)*
:::

::: {.tej-visual-card}
![Close view of a twisted-pair Ethernet cable and modular plug.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/file/Ethernet_cable_closeup.JPG)

### Read the jacket

Look for the category, conductor type, and certification printed along the cable jacket.

*Figure 2. [Open source and licence.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ethernet_cable_closeup.JPG)*
:::
::::

::: {.tej-category-grid}
<div><strong>Cat5e</strong>1 Gbps to 100 m. 2.5 or 5 Gbps may work when the equipment and cable meet the standard.</div>
<div><strong>Cat6</strong>1 Gbps to 100 m. 10 Gbps on shorter runs, commonly up to 55 m in suitable conditions.</div>
<div><strong>Cat6A</strong>10 Gbps to 100 m. Thicker and often less flexible.</div>
<div><strong>Cat8</strong>25 or 40 Gbps to 30 m. Mainly data centres, not a normal classroom patch cable.</div>
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What about Cat7?"}
Cat7 appears in retail listings, but it is not the normal ANSI/TIA category choice for a standard RJ45 classroom cable. Prefer a correctly made Cat6 or Cat6A cable for a known requirement.
:::

**Class choice:** use the cable and plug specified by the teacher. Match the plug to solid or stranded conductors and to the cable diameter.
